utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Ms. Mahindaratne, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And before we continue, do you know whether you or the witness applies for protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution is not applying for protective measures because we do not have instructions from the witness; however, the witness indicated that he may seek protective measures, and for that reason, if we could go into private session when we walks into the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, private session would not do, I take it. It depends on what kind of protective measures the witness is seeking. I, therefore, suggest that we would have to go into closed session, out of an abundance of caution, unless -- in this situation where this is an indication that there may be an application by the witness himself or herself to apply for protective measures, the most safe way of proceeding would be to ask the witness in closed session. I do not hear of any objections; therefore, we turn into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber would like to make a short statement with regard to you, Mr. Mikulicic, as Defence counsel for Mr. Markac. This statement is about your relationship, if any, with the next witness, Mr. Celic. The Prosecution is seeking to tender a suspect interview which was held on the 25th and the 26th of November, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said, the Prosecution is seeking to tender a suspect interview held with the witness on the 25th and the 26th of November, 2002, pursuant to Rule 92 ter. During this interview, Mr. Mikulicic, you were representing the witness. The Chamber has been informed that the parties have exchanged views about this by e-mail. And according to this exchange, Mr. Mikulicic, you have explained that you were only representing this witness during the said interview and that you had had no contact with him since then; and, therefore, you consider that there is no conflict of interest. The Chamber expresses some concern in relation to the position you've taken, but perhaps even more about the explanation you have given, because, as far as the Chamber is -- on the basis of the interpretation of your obligations as Defence counsel and, of course, I'm primarily referring to the Code of Professional Conduct, Article 14, it is not only a matter whether you have any contact with the witness up till today, it is also a matter of whether you obtained any information when you still had contact with the witness that would be useful for the Defence of Mr. Markac, but you would be prevented from revealing such information, due to your obligation of confidentiality in relation to the witness. And, of course, that dilemma, if would you have such information, which you might be under an obligation to keep for yourself and not use for your present client, that would, of course, also block you in sharing that information with Mr. Kuzmanovic, for example. The Chamber is aware that the matter raised is a question which only you can answer. I bring to your attention that the Chamber had some concerns reading your explanation why there was no conflict of interest, because the Chamber, interpreting your obligations here, thinks that the analysis should be slightly different and should include also whether or not you of received, from the witness, any information you could not use because there would be the conflict of interest, and not whether you had contact with the witness at any later stage. That, for the Chamber, at least, seems not to be the right test. At the same time, you are the only one who can answer that question; and, therefore, we just bring this to your attention and we would urge you to act in such a manner that would safeguard the integrity of these proceedings. So I'm not saying what you should do because the basic question is whether you ever gained such information, an element which was not included in your explanation, that there was no conflict of interest. Therefore, the Chamber has addressed you on this matter. This concludes the statement of the Chamber in this respect. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, would you like me to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we take it that if any such information would be at your disposal, that you would act accordingly. Even answering the question, whether you received information of this kind and to what extent it would block you, might already be a breach of confidentiality. So the Chamber is not seeking an answer to that. The Chamber has drawn your attention to what the Chamber considered not to be a full and complete analysis of the situation --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and urges you to include in your considerations the matter that we have just brought to your attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, I appreciate your explanation. The only thing I could say at that very moment is that I'm always behaving myself as an officer of the court, and I will always have in mind that if something that occurred that could jeopardize my position in this proceeding, I will surely raise this question before the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. It is a mixed issue. It relates both to your position as an officer of the court and also to your position as a faithful servant to the interest of your clients. I have made this statement on behalf of the Chamber, and I'd like to proceed. I thought it better not to raise the issue in the presence of the witness. Of course, Mr. Markac was entitled to be present during this statement. Ms. Mahindaratne, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Celic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. Celic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require to you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration, of which the text will now be handed out to you by Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Celic. Please be seated. Mr. Celic, you will first be examined by Ms. Mahindaratne who is counsel for the Prosecution. Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Celic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I'm Josip Celic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I work in the mobile unit of the traffic police at the police directorate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And were you within the special police sector before you came into the present branch?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Before I was transferred to this job, for 14 years, I worked in the anti-terrorist unit, Lucko, of the special police.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in 1995, what position within the Lucko Unit did you hold?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I was assistant commander of the anti-terrorist unit, Lucko.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In 2001, were you appointed as the commander of the Lucko Unit?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And thereafter, at some stage, did you cease to hold that position?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes. I was transferred to another job.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: That was in 2004.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, on 25th and 26th November, 2002, were you interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor as a suspect in the investigation relating to this case?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And was that interview conducted in the ICTY Zagreb field office?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Were you informed at that stage that you had certain rights, one of which was to be represented in the course of the interview by an attorney of your choice?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And were you represented by Mr. Goran Mikulicic, who is present in court today, in the -- during the entire course of that interview?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was that interview conducted via an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When the members of the Office of the Prosecutor asked you questions in the course of that interview, did you answer those questions truthfully?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I did my best to remember the whole truth. I pointed out several times that I could not say exactly what the time was, but did I my best to tell the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And was that interview video-recorded?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And at the completion of the interview, were copies of the video-recorded interview handed over to your attorney?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, again, Mr. Celic, in 2005, 13th and 14th January, 2005, were you interviewed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor for a second time as a suspect in this case?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was that interview also conducted in the Zagreb field office, ICTY?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And were you represented in the -- during the entire course of that interview by an attorney of your choice?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And was the interview conducted via an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when the members of the Office of the Prosecutor asked you questions at that time - this is the second interview - did you answer those questions truthfully?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was that interview video-recorded?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And at the completion of the interview, were copies of the video records handed over to your attorney?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Celic, if you were asked those questions that were asked of you by the members of the Office of the Prosecutor in January 2002 -- I'm sorry, in November 2002 and January 2005, today here in court, would your answers be the same? And when I say that, I'm not talking about the language and the words, but would the content and the substance of the answers be the same as those you provided in the course of those interviews?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Basically, yes, of course. However, I would like to point out that between the first and second interview, since quite a bit of time had elapsed, I could not say what the exact time difference was in terms of what had happened. So, during the second interview, perhaps the time-frame was somewhat different than during the first interview. However, I have been doing my best all along to tell the truth, the whole truth, and everything as best I remembered it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Celic. I'll just quickly bring up the two videos so you can just identify a couple of seconds of each, so you could identify in Court that they are, indeed, the interviews.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could play 4124.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, I'll just play a little bit, just the first few seconds, and can you identify whether this is, indeed, the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is that the video recording --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Please keep playing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: -- of the interview in 2002?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Could you play 5274, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, was that the video recording of the second interview in 2005 that was shown on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to move into evidence the video tapes of the two recordings with the corresponding transcripts, and there are three tapes for the 2002 interview and three tapes for 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have provided Mr. Registrar with the relevant 65 ter numbers?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. For the record, I will read it out: 65 ter 5384 for the 2002 interview, which comprises of three tapes, V000-4124, 4125, and 4126; and the 2005 interview is 65 ter number 5385, comprising of three tapes, V000-5274, 5275, and 5276, with the corresponding transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If I remember will, there are no objections by any of the Defence times. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, the 2002 interview, 5384, would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P761.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P761, including video and transcript, is admitted into evidence. And the 2005 interview, 5385, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That becomes Exhibit number P762, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P762, in the absence of any objections, is admitted into evidence. Further, Ms. Mahindaratne, I just use the opportunity that there was an application to add some documents to your 65 ter list. From all Defence teams, we received information that there is it no objection to that, so that request is granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I be permitted to have two binders of the transcripts handed over to the witness. It's with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Usher, would you please provide the binders to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, while that is being done, before we proceed, there are three corrections to be made in the English transcripts - it's correct in the B/C/S - if I could just read that into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you then allow me for one second to get the ... Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There's a correction to be made in P761 - that's the 2002 interview - section 2. That is 4125 at page 9. The name "Zdravko Janic" has been recorded as "Ratko Mladic." The same mistake has been made at page 16, too. This is only in the English transcript. The second correction is again in P761, part 3. That is 4126, page 21. There's a reference to "HRT" which should be corrected as "HTV." This correct term is in the B/C/S version. The third correction is in P762, the 2005 interview, part 3, page 193. There's a name "Stakic"; it should be correct the as "Sacic." Those are the corrections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought that it's just a matter of translation, transcribing, and that it doesn't change the original; so, therefore, I didn't ask whether there were any objections. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call for document P558, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, you have been provided with two binders, and they're clearly marked as to which is the 2002 transcripts and the other one is 2005. And in each of those binders, there are three parts, so as we go I refer to each part and you could turn to that. Now, your testimony is that on 24th August, 1995, the Lucko Unit commander Mr. Turkalj called you and gave you an order regarding the Oluja-Obruc mop-up operation. That's correct, isn't it? It is already stated by you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you will see a document on the screen. Do you recognise that document? Is that the order that was given to you by Mr. Turkalj?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Pursuant to this order, you commanded on the ground, you were the ground commander for two operations; that is, on 25th, in the Plavno valley and the second one on the Knin-Drnis road in the area in front of the -- in the area of the Promina hills.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the course of those two operations, whom did you report to as your overall operation commander?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Mr. Zdravko Janic, the head of the department for combatting terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, can I have document P559, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Celic, in the course of the interview, you identified the map that was used for the operation on the 25th, and if you could identify the map on the screen. It will take a while. You, in fact, identified the axis of the Lucko Unit on that map. Is that the map that was used for the operation on the 25th?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you -- in your transcripts, you identified the axis of the Lucko Unit as that line that starts with LATJ.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: With the communication in the -- or the road in the valley, the main road in the valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And according to this map, the Lucko Unit is -- was the only unit was to go through the area covering Grubori, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: When we're talking about in depth, the situation in depth, then the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Just to clarify, in the interview, you were asked to identify what that area is which is marked as a tie, and testimony was that's the area which was marked as having a bigger probability of having terrorists. Now, in relation to that, if you could just point out where Grubori is.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if you could give a pointer to Mr. Celic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the right colour which is --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. I believe, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- blue for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could just mark --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Red for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If could you just mark --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could just focus on that area, can we have a close-up. That area that indicates as a tie, you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the witness starts marking, let's have the map zoomed in such a way, then perhaps you would guide, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If we could just -- can you note the figure 25 in red. If you start from north and if you come down, that's right. If you take it up a little bit further, yes, that's right. Then take it to east, to your right, that's right. If you could just -- yeah, that's correct. That should do.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, can you identify Grubori on the map? I could assist you if you -- but I think you would be far more familiar with this map than me.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this map is already in evidence; however, this marked map, does it get a new number or does it remain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. The marked map receives a new number, but I missed the marking, Ms. Mahindaratne, so could you assist me. Is that just to the left of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's to the -- it's more towards west, to the west of that area which is marked as a tie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we make the marking a bit more clear, because now it seems to be lost more or less in other red markings which are there already. Could the witness perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, could you sort of make it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- enlarge it or put a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Can you please circle around that marking you just made?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now it becomes more clear. No more markings?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Could that get some sort of exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P763.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P763 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, your testimony was -- I will read it to you, if you could turn to the 2005 transcript, part 2, page 55. You stated that -- I'm reading your -- on that page, the second answer, and about four lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. Page 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 55. Now, I see we have two different sets of pages. First of all, if we open the rather lengthy document of 679 pages in the Adobe format, then, of course, we have consecutive numbering; whereas, if you refer to the numbering of the various tapes, then it starts with each new tape and new numbering starts. Could you always clearly indicate whether we are in 4124, 4125, and what page we are so that we can find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I will go by the ERN also. I'm referring to specifically the 2005 interview. That is P762, part 2; that is V000-5275; and page 55.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President? Have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I believe it should be an interview from 2002, and not 2005.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If I could take to you 2005, the second tape, that is V000-5275 - I think Mr. Celic has found it - if we go even by the 92 ter submission. It's page 55, and it starts with a B/C/S answer -- sorry, B/C/S interpretation there. Mr. President, do you have the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I don't. I have not found it yet, but I have to find my way through there almost 680 pages, which we have all kind of -- what I would prefer, as a matter of fact, that since it has been tendered as one annex to your motion at the time, that you refer to the overall paging, which means somewhere between 1 and 679. Otherwise we have to find the section exactly which matches with your numbers. Sometimes we find them at the bottom, sometimes we find them at the top, then we have to find the right section, and then within that section the page number; whereas, this is an overall paging covering everything. But I take it that have you not been prepared for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, because in the 92 ter submission, we -- I do believe we paginated from 1 to 600. What we did was we submitted the -- the transcripts in three separate sections. I think on the e-court, though, what happened was one 65 ter number was given to all three transcripts, all three sections, of a particular transcript. So unless you're following the e-court -- is that what you're following, Mr. President, or do you have the hard copy of the transcripts with you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Printing 700 pages where you can look at them on the screen three times, that's 2.000 pages, that is a half a wood spent on printing. So we are working from the e-court version.

utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, this is what you say: "All group commanders were required to inform me if they encountered armed resistance. Nobody called me and reported anything of that sort to me." Now, you're talking about the operation in Plavno on the 25th. There you go on to say, the next answer: "Once they arrived at the final destination, they reported to me verbally that nothing had happened." Then if could I ask to you go down a few pages, down to page 58. This is your first response on that page, and the last two lines, where you said: "On the contrary, when they arrived at the end point, they all reported to me that nothing had happened, that there had been no interventions." Then, further down, on page 64, if you could turn to page 64, you say, and this is your first response: "While I was waiting for them at the end point, I recall that I had already started writing the report that I was writing based on the map. I just needed information of their arrival time and whether there had been any interventions during the operation and which ones." Then a few lines down, you say: "As these people told me that there were no interventions at that time, that everything was all right, I already had the report. And I added that in the course of the operation, the unit did not encounter any resistance; and when we arrived in Gracac, I submitted that report." So this is an obvious question, but since it has not been properly stated. Now, that report, what exactly did it say? Because we don't have that report here, and I'm referring to the original report when your group commanders had reported that nothing had happened and there were no interventions. What did your report say? Was it consistent with what the group leaders said, or did you write -- report something else?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: What it states in the report is the following: On the 25th of August, at such-and-such a time, we received an assignment to search the terrain from the first to the last line. The line is described where the place is -- described; and then the report at the end, which means that when the assignment was set, there were no interventions and that was the end of the report. So the substance of the report was that when the task was carried out, nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you were interviewed in 2002, Mr. Celic, you indicated that you may have had a copy of that report. But in 2005, you were not certain about that, and you did inform the members of the Office of the Prosecutor that you would be able to find a copy and provide it to us. Now, do you have a copy of that original report with you, either here or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: The report was supposed to be in the archive, or rather, should be in the archives of either the command or the unit. I don't know whether they sent it to you and whether they found it at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you have a copy with you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you look in the special police archives whether there was -- this report was there, either in preparation to come for this -- for your testimony or before that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I never went into the archives.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call for document P560, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, now, your testimony was that you submitted this report to the operation headquarters. And you believe that you handed it over to Mr. Janic. Now, we will see -- I appreciate you may or may not have seen this report that's on the screen. Do you recognise this report? Have you seen this report before?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we could move to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you note, Mr. Celic, this is an --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Page 2 of the English version also, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: This is an report on the Lucko Unit's activities on the 25th; this is submitted by Mr. Janic. Now, is this consistent with the -- with the original report that you submitted to Mr. Janic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Celic, I'm going to ask you a series of questions about matters you're familiar with; and so that we don't waste much time, let me, once and for all, take you to that part of your testimony. If you could turn to 2005 interview.

utterances.text: That is P762, for the record.

utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, if would you give me the numbers under which the documents were filed, they are sequentially numbered, then I would have no problems in finding it in the electronic version. So the --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... at the top of the pages, if you give me that number, I will find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It is 2005; that's P762, part 2; that would be 5275, and page 70.

utterances.text: Which is, Mr. President, page 13467; that's page 70 of 112.

utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, you were asked this question: "Okay. When was the first you heard that obviously there had been a problem in the village of Grubori?" And your response is: "I said last time, as well. I believe it was the next day. I'm not sure but I believe it was the next day. Mr. Sacic and Mr. Markac called me to the headquarters, and that was the first time I found out that something had happened there."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could go down two pages down to page 72, that is in the same section, page 72, two pages down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You say: "I believe I was personally called by Mr. Janic or somebody from headquarters -- or somebody from the headquarters to report to Mr. Sacic or Mr. Markac." "You don't remember to contacted you? "I couldn't be -- I'm not sure -- 100 percent sure. "But you say you were called and you had to report to General Markac and Mr. Sacic? "They had called me to inform me that something had happened. They already had my report. That was the first time I had learned that something had happened." And, Mr. Celic, if you could go down three pages, to page 75, where you were asked: "Did you go to where they set up their command in Gracac? "That is right. "Did anyone accompany you to go and see Mr. Sacic and Mr. Markac? "As far as I remember, no." Then the next page: "And when you arrived there, were you seen by both of them, Mr. Markac and Mr. Sacic? "Yes, and there was an additional gentleman who was there, too. "Okay. Who was that? "Mr. Pavlovic from the communications department. He was in the headquarters in charge of communications."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, when you are reading --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- your speed of speech goes up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And before I ask you the question, Mr. Celic, I'd like to also show you your 2002 interview on this same issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is P761, part 2, which is 4125, page 40.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in your version, which is the B/C/S version --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Ms. Mahindaratne. That, Your Honour, is page 13791.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, in the B/C/S version, it is page 37. Have you found it? And in the English version, it starts at the bottom, page 40. I will read it, then you'll know, Mr. Celic, where we are: "I believe that it was the next day. I'm not sure. I cannot say exactly what time. I was called by General Markac and Mr. Sacic, when they called me and told me that I had submitted a report which said that nothing had happened and that they had information that something had happened, to which I answered ..." --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's going on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Page 41: "... with which I answered that that was the report I got from my group leaders or group commanders. And they told me there was nothing; and in case there was something, they should call them and ask them. And I can't say exactly how long the conversation lasted, but after that they told me to write a new report, another report." In terms what time this was, you say: "I cannot say for sure, but I think it was before 9.00." Now, if you move to the next page in the English transcript, you were asked the question: "When you were told this by Mr. Markac and Sacic, that an incident happened, did they tell you what had happened? "They told me that there was an armed conflict. I don't remember now the exact words they used, but there was an armed conflict, and something had happened there and that I wrote in my report that there was nothing." Then you go on to say - and you are probably with what you said, Mr. Celic - that from there you were taken to another room and the report was dictated to you by Mr. Sacic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, if we could have document P563, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, your testimony was, Mr. Celic, that in that other room, Mr. Sacic dictated to you a second report to be submitted in relation to the incident; and parts of what you were supposed to write were written by Mr. Sacic on the reverse of your original report, which is the report that we don't have. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: What you said -- well, I would like to differentiate between two points. With respect to the event itself, I can describe to you -- well, I believe Mr. Zdravko Janic called me to the headquarters; and at the headquarters, General Markac was there and Mr. Sacic was there. And at that first interview, they asked me what happened -- what actually happened because they probably expected that I knew something. However, at that point in time, the only thing I did know was that nothing had happened. And after that -- so you mention something about them taking me into another room. That's not true. I went with Mr. Sacic to the operative part, to another area, and I wrote the report with him. So not with Mr. Markac and Mr. Sacic, but only with Mr. Sacic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... say that "they" took you, but what I told you was what you have exactly us, and I can read what you said. But what I asked you was -- well, your testimony so far is that Markac and Sacic spoke to you, and you were asked to write another report. Then Mr. Sacic took you from there to another room, and he dictated a new report to you. That was your testimony. My question was -- you have said that in the course of that new report being dictated, Mr. Sacic also wrote parts of what you were supposed to write on the reverse of your original report. Now, my question was: Is that the one that is missing today, the one that we don't have here, but the one that you said might be in the special police archives? Did you understand what I said?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: The report is correct. But let me emphasise once again and don't misunderstand me, but the interpreter keeps using the plural saying that "they" took me away and that "they" dictated to me. I was only with Mr. Sacic and not with Mr. Markac. But that's the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yeah. My question to you is: When you were taken from that room where you spoke to Mr. Markac and Sacic, you were taken out of that room by Mr. Sacic to another room and the report was dictated to you. Is that correct? Well, let me read what you have said about that, so that there is no further confusion.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: As far as the report is concerned, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes. My question to you is this -- you were asked this: "As a result of what you had said, did they still tell you that you had -- you have to got to do a new report? "Yes."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. It is it, again, at 2002, the same section we were in, 2002; P761, section 2, 4125, page 43.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's the section I was reading on, Mr. Celic, if you could follow this when I read this. You were asked a question: "As a result of what you had said, did they still tell that you have got to do a new report? "Yes. "Did they tell you that you got to do it on your own? "It was dictated to me. "Okay. By whom? "Sacic. "Okay. Was that after you had spoken to your four group leaders? When he dictated it to you, had you had a chance to speak to your four group leaders, before you had -- you heard what Mr. Sacic had to say? "No. "So, in fact, he repeated -- the fact the report that was dictated to you by Sacic, basically you had no knowledge of what he was telling you? "No. "So were you put in a very difficult position? And after he had dictated this report to you, were you obliged to sign it? "Yes. I wrote it and I signed it." And if you could go to section 3, that is 4126.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That is, again, 2002, 4126, page 2. Mr. Cayley, are you able to -- that is section of 3 of 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. That is page 13785.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You were asked this question, Mr. Celic: "When it was mentioned that you -- mentioned to you that you got to do another report, was Mr. Markac present? " Your response is: "Yes." Then: "Who actually told you got to do a new report? "After that conversation, that talk, I went with Mr. Sacic to a separate -- to another room, and that's where I had to do -- I had to write it." Then you were asked the last question: "Okay. And your report was handwritten, was it? "Yes." So your evidence that that is what I, in fact, asked you, that I didn't mix it up. My question was this: Now your evidence is clear you spoke with Mr. Markac and Sacic, you were asked to write another report, Sacic took you to another room, and you wrote a new report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if we go down a few pages down, that is the same section, page 93. I'm sorry. This is 2005, 2005, section 3; that is 5276.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, if you could look at the 2005 interview, your second interview. Not the first one; the second interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, excuse me, Ms. Mahindaratne. Your Honour, that is page 1331 -- I'm sorry. It is page 13331.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you look at the third part, Mr. Celic, and if you move to actually page 94, you say this: "In your report that you say was dictated by Mr. Sacic, you mention a prisoner. "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If I may have a minute, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I find the prisoner on line 21 of this page 94, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I was trying to really find another section. Anyway, let me move on without wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Sacic dictated the new report to you, did he or did you have a copy, or did he have the original of your original report, the one that you submitted that that there was no incident? You know, in your first report where you said there was no intervention, was that report there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What did Mr. Sacic do with that report, did you see? Did you leave it in his custody? Did you bring it back? What happened to that report, your original report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: That report was handed in a day earlier. Now, whether it was photocopied or not, I don't know. I believe it was. He showed me the report at the moment when we wrote the new report, when I was supposed to write the new report. I had this report in front of me because from that report, I got out information concerning the directions involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yeah. My question is: Once the new report was written, what did Mr. Sacic do with your old report, the one that we do not have here today and you said might be in the special police archives? That's what I'm asking you. The old report, what did Mr. Sacic do with the old report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I won't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, can we try to have this clarified. You said Mr. Sacic showed you the report. It was in front of you because you took some information from that. Did you take it at the end? Did Mr. Sacic take it with him at the end? Did anyone else take it with him when you had written your new report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that that report, together with all other reports, was in the same file and that it does exist somewhere in the archives. Now, whether there was a copy or whether there was an original, I'm confident that that was the original and that a copy exists, too, and I believe that this report is somewhere in the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was a different one. I'd like to take you back it that room where you write your second report and where the original report was in front of you. Who took those papers with him when you left that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I left the documents there. Who took them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Celic, do you note the document on the screen. Do you -- can you recognise it? That's a report written by you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes, this is my second report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Is this the report that was dictated to you by Mr. Sacic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, your testimonies at the time Mr. Sacic dictated this report to you, when you wrote this report, you did not know or you were not aware of this incident, nor did you know any of these details. So did you ever raise it with him or ask him as to why you were being asked to write these details when you don't even know about it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Well, actually, at that point in time, I knew that nothing had happened. Since he was my superior, not for a moment did I think that what he was saying was not the truth. He had full authority as far as I was concerned, and I acted on orders, I wrote out the report as he told me to do, and I did not check the information involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you ask him from where he got that information, based on what he was dictating this incident to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, at the time, Mr. Markac was in the same building, wasn't he? You had just met him before you went to this other room with Mr. Sacic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: After the -- after leaving the room where they were together, I did not see Mr. Markac. Maybe he was in the building; maybe he went out into the field. I don't know. It is possible that he was indoors; it is possible that he left from the moment when we parted. I did not see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, after this -- after writing this second report, did you ever meet with Mr. Markac and ask him why you were made to write a report that you had no knowledge about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I did meet him many times, but we never talked about that. At that moment, Mr. Sacic, who was chief of sector, gave me this information, and I did not doubt it. I had no reason not to believe him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: But going to that part I was going to read to you earlier on, you were the commander on the ground of that operation. In your experience, is it possible that units -- or your unit could meet with resistance and an event, as described in this report, could take place without that being reported to you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: That was not supposed to happen, but obviously it did happen. None of the leaders of the groups who were out in the field informed me about an armed conflict. So, if there were a conflict at any point in time, it was their duty to report to me as to what was going on. I did not receive this information. On the contrary, I received information from all group leaders that nothing had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when Mr. Sacic was dictating this to you, he gives details about a prisoner what was taken; and, in fact, the name of this prisoner is also given. As the operation commander, you were aware that no prisoners were taken in the operation. Now, did that fact at least not lead you to realize at that time that you were being asked to write a false report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: As for detainees, prisoners, I did not see any prisoners at any point in time and there weren't any. I would have known. I would have either -- or rather, they would have taken them to the line, and they were document bound do tell me about this. There were no prisoners. Now, whether some other unit entered our area, whether they had prisoners, I don't know. At that moment, I did not think about that. I trusted Mr. Sacic. I believe what he said. It was a large area. There were a lot of units there. And quite simply, at that point in time, I believe that things were the way he had put them. Not at any moment did I doubt what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time is this a good time to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Ms. Mahindaratne. Could I ask, however, one clarifying question. You said, "There were a lot of units there." What units are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if we were to return the map, I could tell you. The map shows what units were there: Osijek, Split. I'm speaking for memory now. I don't know if there was Rijeka or something else. But it is evident on the map what units were there. You can see that on the map, about 500 to 600 men, four or five units. However, we can always see that on the basis o from the report from Chief Janic. I remember Osijek, Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let me ask you: The report is talking about the unit which I understand to be your unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, therefore, if you said perhaps another unit may have taken someone prisoner, the report reflects that the unit which you said is your unit took prisoners. I'm asking you this because you said, Well, it might have been another unit, but the report states that it was the unit, which means, in this context, your unit. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I wanted to say in relation to prisoners that our point of departure and our ending point were the same. All units came to this ending point, like we did. And I wanted to say I don't know whether other units had prisoners, but I wanted to point out that our unit certainly did not have any prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the new report states that prisoners were taken by your unit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Obviously, this information is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, and everyone else, we will have a break, and we resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may I have P566, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, now, your testimony was that after this, you know, writing of the report on the 26th with Mr. Sacic, once you went to Zagreb, Mr. Turkalj ordered you and the four group leaders to submit a report on this incident. And could you see -- do you know the document on the screen? Do you recognise this document? Is this the order that Mr. Turkalj gave you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, as far as you're aware, up until this time - that is, when Mr. Turkalj ordered you and the four group leaders to submit a report - were there any reports that been submitted by anybody who participated in the operation on 25th which supported the version that was dictated to you by Mr. Sacic on 26th? Did you understand what I said?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying. As far as I know, no. No one submitted any reports to me; that is to say, that after the action was offer, I just received a verbal/oral report. I'm the only one who wrote a written report, and I doubt that anyone else did. It is possible that I am not aware of that; but, as far as I know, no one else did.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: May I have, Mr. Registrar, document P564, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Celic, your evidence was that in response to Mr. Turkalj's order, you submitted a typed version of the same report that you hand-wrote when Mr. Sacic dictated. Now, is this the report that you submitted in response to Mr. Turkalj; that is, a typed version of your handwritten previous report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you -- your testimony is that you submitted this in response to Mr. Turkalj's order which was dated 1st September, as we just saw it. Why did you back date this report to the 25th, instead of inserting the correct date? Because if this was submitted in response to the 1st September order, it should be the 1st September or a date thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I just copied the report that had been written on the 26th of August. The report that I wrote on the 26th of August is also dated the 25th of August, and I thought that that report was identical. I inserted the same date. I had no special reason not to put this date, or any other date for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did anyone instruct to you back date this report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, this report is identical in content to your handwritten report that we saw earlier, with the exception that in your handwritten report, there is the last line says that: "The task was completed at 1600 hours and that no one was injured or wounded." That line has been omitted from the report. Was there any particular reason why you omitted the timing the operation was completed from this report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: There was absolutely no reason, except for this report that have you here, there is yet another report that differs, in terms of a particular section, because I was the first one to write a report out in the field. This is the typed up version. There is no reason for the change. However, on the basis of this report that had been typed out, the group leaders, in accordance with the commander's order, had to submit reports as well. After they did that, they inserted a section which was truthful, of course, and I said how civilians should be treated. That is what I said at the point of departure. In Gracac, I did not include that after their reports were written up, then this section was included in my report. So then there's this other report that differs from that point of view. But the question that you put to me, well, there was no reason why the time was not inserted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So, following what you just said, it was after you submitted this report that the group leaders submitted their reports on the incident, the typed versions.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And since you mentioned the other report with the extra paragraph, I'll call that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have document P565, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, while that document is being brought up, Mr. Celic, I'd like you to look at your 2005 interview. Mr. Celic, if could you look at your 2005 interview, section 2, that is 5275, page 102.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, it is page 13435 on the filed version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, there, you're referring to that -- your next report, which we have just brought up on the screen. You say [sic]: "Okay. Before the break, I asked you to mark the document JC-6, which was, in fact, a document which had an extra paragraph of a report dated 26th August 1995. This is a document that has an extra paragraph in it. This is an extra paragraph relating to the treatment of prisoners, et cetera." And your response is: "That is the same one, I believe. In fact, I know this is the same one that was written that day, except for this: This one was the one that the secretary added this paragraph. It wasn't written later. It was written, I believe, the same day that we were writing the reports in Zagreb." Now, so, my first question is: You submitted that typed version and the group leaders also were there in Zagreb at the time, isn't it, in this office location where you're typing and submitting reports.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And whose secretary was it who inserted that additional paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: All the reports that were handwritten were typed up by the secretary of the commander. Since my report was written first, after that, it was the group leaders who wrote their reports. I believe, since she had typed this out, that the group leaders actually wrote the reports; and then after that, well, that was true. That paragraph was quite true. That is the only thing I added to my own report, and this was typed up by the secretary; that is to say, she did the typing for all of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, when you say the "secretary of the commander," whom are you referring to? Who was the commander? Whom are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: When I'm talking about "the commander," I'm just talking about the commander of my unit, Mr. Turkalj.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what the witness said before that, due to background noise.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, could you repeat what you said. The interpreter could not hear. You said something. Could you repeat your response?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: When I'm talking about "the commander," I'm talking only about the commander of my unit, Mr. Josip Turkalj.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So it was his secretary that inserted this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: That's right, and I do believe that I said that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And who instructed her to insert this paragraph? I'm not challenging the veracity of the content of that paragraph, Mr. Celic, I'm just asking who instructed her to insert that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I do believe that that was me, since she wrote all the reports and she knew who wrote what. And the leader of the groups all wrote that, and without a doubt that was the truth. And when that was typed out, when they all tabled the report, I probably said that that portion should be put into my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, the content of this report is identical to your handwritten report that you wrote, which was dictated to you by Mr. Sacic. Now, did the secretary have a copy of that ? Did you bring in a copy? How is that the secretary ended up typing an identical report with identical content as your handwritten report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: She copied it out from the report that I wrote and brought in. I don't want to misspeak. The possibility does exist that I brought it with me, and there is also the possibility that it was returned to us. But I do believe I brought it with me because, according to the operative assignment in the field, it was my duty to submit a report in the field. But I'm also duty-bound to report to the commander about the engagement of the unit, so I do believe that I probably had a copy of that report myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So the secretary basically copied or looked at your handwritten report and typed out the two versions that we looked at, the typed versions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: She either looked at it or I read it out, but it's the same contents, the some contents from the same report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look at -- in your 2005 interview, Mr. Celic, if could you go to part 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And this is 5276, page 46; that is the filed version, page 13377.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you said the group leaders also wrote reports, and you go on to say your response there: "Of course, I saw them because the secretary wrote all the reports; and I probably, as I read those reports, I saw that individual people had written that paragraph and that version without that addition might have already been printed. And after I saw that, I cannot confirm whether all the members had written that or just some; but after that, I added this paragraph." So at this place, while these reports were being written, obviously, it seems that there has been a comparison of reports, your report vis-a-vis the reports of the group leaders for -- to ensure consistency. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes. I did have an insight in all -- into all the reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And it was at that stage that addition was taken to have this additional paragraph inserted into the reports, yours and the four group leaders -- I'm sorry, three group leaders' reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: As for me, yes, but I do believe they already had it written down. I am sure that some of the leaders of the groups had written that down, so we wrote it on that basis, because if we didn't have it, I don't believe that I would have added it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, at the time these reports were being submitted, was there a discussion amongst you and the group leaders as to why they informed you previously at the end of the operation that there were no interventions, and now, here, you are writing a completely different report on the incident? It is logical that there would have been a discussion, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Correct. On the basis of this order and even before that, together with Commander Turkalj we were in the Grubori area itself, and we saw for ourselves that something had happened. Now, the commander asked, on the basis of these written reports, asked what had happened. I had nothing to state in that portion because I know that nothing happened. And the leader of the group -- the leaders of the group tabled the report, but we didn't discuss it so I had nothing to say. I was just given the possibility of saying that they conveyed to me that nothing had happened. And after that, I wrote the report with Mr. Sacic, in which I set out all these facts, the facts contained in the report; and after that, all the group leaders had to write whether anything happened, and what happened, and who knew what. But let me state once again that, at first, I didn't know that anything had happened. Quite the contrary, I knew that everything was quite all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm not contesting that, Mr. Celic. My point is, firstly, did you ask the group leaders at this time -- because you were the first to write the report when Mr. Sacic dictated it to you. Did you ask them if they reported this, that there was something happening, to Mr. Sacic or whether they had reported it to someone else other than yourself? Did they tell you that they had spoken with Mr. Sacic before you spoke with Mr. Sacic on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Nobody told me, and I'm quite convinced that nobody had spoken to them. That's my opinion. But the best thing would be for you to ask him because I can't really say. I'm quite convinced that nobody talked about it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So, as far as you knew, when Mr. Sacic dictated the report to you, the group leaders had not talked to Mr. Sacic or informed him this or any incident in Grubori?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. You already asked this question, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I don't think I did, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness answered it already. You didn't ask. As a matter of fact, you asked the witness to enter into a debate with you on what was logical under the circumstances, yes or no. So apart from putting a leading question and the Defence apparently did not object, then you even added to that what you would consider to be the logical answer, which I would invite you to refrain from doing. Then the witness said it was his opinion that no one had talked to Mr. Sacic when Mr. Sacic dictated the report, which is to be understood as that this witness certainly has no knowledge that he did, because otherwise he could not have expressed that opinion as being the whole truth. So, to that extent, Mr. Mikulicic is to some extent right that the witness has already included in his answer --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... the previous answer, the answer to your question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have document P572, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, while that document is being brought up, Mr. Balunovic, one of the group leaders, is a close friend of yours, isn't it? This is an close friendship. You said that in your testimony. That is why I suggested that to you.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Could I ask you to repeat the surname, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You know, the group leader, Balunovic. I will give you the exact name.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: You probably mean Balunovic, Balunovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry if my pronunciation wasn't right. Yes. He is the person I'm referring to, one of the group leaders of Lucko Unit. Now, was there a close friendship between you and him?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And as such, are you able to recognise his signature by any chance?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Of course, he was my subordinate and I roughly know what his signature looks like.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You, in fact, testified that -- your testimony is that you saw the reports of the group leaders. Can you identify the document on the screen? Have you seen this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could go to the next page, so that Mr. Celic can see the -- see as to who wrote it.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes. I do believe that that is his signature. Sometimes he writes his name out in full, first and last name; sometimes not. But I would say that that was his signature, gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, having seen this report, did you ever ask him why he wrote a report such as this, when his initial report to you on the incident was that nothing had happened; or did you ask him the circumstances under which he submitted this report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: At the time he wrote the report, I know that he was the left flank; and as he was on the left flank, since we were down there together where the incident happened, I was convinced that he knew nothing either. Because two or three days after the event itself, both he and I had to go to Gracac and convince ourselves that something had happened. So by going into the field, in the territory, he didn't know what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... not talking --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: So just by that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. I'm not talking about whether he knew or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if you could, Mr. Registrar, go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In this report, there is -- this is a report on an armed clash. My question to you is: Now, your -- what Mr. Balunovic reported to you at the end of operation was that there were no interventions, there was no resistance whatsoever; however, this report has a reference to an armed clash. So did you not ask him why he didn't say so previously, if there had been armed clash; or why he is now submit ago different report? Did you ever have that conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: That's precisely what I wanted to tell you. Before writing the report, together with Mr. Balunovic, I was duty-bound to go to Gracac to the very spot, to the very locality; and during that arrival, nobody knew what had happened. At that point in time, he, too, was convinced that nothing had happened. But, afterwards, when we went down there and when we saw that something had happened, we wrote the report and Branko Balunovic wrote the report stating that something had in actual fact happened. So I do believe that what he said after the action itself, after the action was completed, was truthful; that is to say, that he did not know what had happened because that's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So when you say you went up there and saw something had happened, what you mean is that you're referring, in fact, to your visit to Grubori with Mr. Balunovic and Mr. Turkalj, isn't it? That's what you're referring to, that's when you saw three bodies and some houses had been burned, that's what you just referred to, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: That's right. But that's the answer to your question about why Branko Balunovic didn't tell me that something had happened immediately after the action. That means we went back to Zagreb after the action. From Zagreb, we went down there once again and discussed it, talked about. And during that conversation, he kept telling me that nothing had happened. So, then, he knew nothing right up until the point that we got there. That's what I wanted to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So, what you're saying is having visited Grubori and seeing the three bodies - you said you saw only three bodies in your testimony - and having seen the burnt houses, then you realized that something had happened and you came back to Zagreb, and then these reports were written. That's your testimony. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Let me clarify this about the report. I was the only one who wrote the report before, the second day, on the 22nd [as interpreted], in Gracac itself, when we talked about something having happened; and then I believe that something really did happen. However, I personally saw the dead bodies myself and saw what had happened, but the report had already been written before I had seen that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, it's been recorded as 22nd --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am sorry. Just for the sake of correction, in the transcript, it was written that the second day was "the 22nd," which is obviously not what witness said. It was "26th."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's what I was trying to say, yes. It's the 26th, Mr. President. It is not contested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, not contested. Ms. Mahindaratne, I noticed that you put the question to the witness several times which apparently there was some communication problem perhaps. Mr. Celic, what Ms. Mahindaratne apparently wants to hear from you is the following: It was reported to you, initially, that nothing had happened. You told us that Mr. Balunovic reported this and that you were convinced that this is what he observed on that day. Now, what Ms. Mahindaratne would like to know, as far as I understand, is that whether you ever discussed with Mr. Balunovic, being a good friend of yours, what happened that at a later stage he writes and signs a report, which is quite different from what he reported to you and what you believed to be what he observed, whether you ever discussed this new report giving all kinds of not only of information which is inconsistent with the first report, but also gives all kind of details, which might be difficult to state on the basis of the observations apparently Mr. Balunovic made on the day itself. Did you ever discuss this with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, and I'll try and make myself clear. We discussed it on the day when, in fact, he -- when we received an order to report down there to see what had happened. Now, on the way to Grubori and Gracac, he was still convinced that nothing had happened, and that is the oral report he gave to me, after the action itself. So, at that point in time, he said he knew that nothing had happened. That's what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But later he produces a report in which it's not only stated that something had happened, which you are convinced he did not observe himself, and gives further details on matters, names on matters which, according to your testimony, he had not observed himself either. So did you at any later stage discuss with him why he wrote and signed a report which you considered could not be based on his personal observations on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked me whether we were good friends. We are good friends, and I really did believe him when he said that nothing had happened. And I believe that his report stemmed from my report, as to the details, because he didn't flow about the names or the years, nor did I know about that, so I wrote what was dictated to me. So I'm convinced that this report of his partially stemmed from the report that I had or the one that I was supposed to write, and I'm convinced also that regardless of the report, he did not know what had happened, or rather, that's what he told me. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of your report, the report that was dictated to you, ever being provided to Mr. Balunovic? Did he tell you, or did you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He must have seen it. I'm convinced -- not convinced. I'm sure that I had that report with me when we were all supposed to write a report, myself and the four group leaders. I must have had the report with me because it was in an identically typed out version, and I wrote my report by hand. I didn't type it out in Gracac. It was written in hand, by hand. And as the secretary wrote the identical report in Zagreb, without a doubt he must have seen my report. He should have seen it, and he must have seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
