utterances.text: So that is a conclusion, he must have seen it because he didn't have the details available to him; but, factually, did you see that it was handed to him, or did you -- I mean, apart from concluding that he must have seen, have you any direct observation on whether it was handed out to him, whether it was in his hands, whether whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say directly, but I can say that we were all invited to the meeting. I am referring to the meeting we had with Commander Turkalj. And since Commander Turkalj and myself and Mr. Balunovic went back from the site of the events, there was a written order asking us all to write a report. And at that point, Mr. Turkalj had my report -- had my report; and, probably, I had my report, too. And Branko Balunovic could have seen it, he could have extracted the details. Now, whether anybody specifically gave it to him, whether did Turkalj or I did, or the secretary, I don't know. The secretary had the report, it was accessible, it wasn't stored in an archive anywhere and not inaccessible. So, whether somebody actually handed to him, perhaps I did, perhaps the secretary did, perhaps the commander did, I can't really say for sure now. But, without a doubt, at that point in time, on that day, he could, anybody could have accessed that document because we didn't have hide anything, the report was on the table for everybody to see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, my last question on the matter: When you were in Zagreb, later, when, as you said, the secretary typed out the reports, can you exclude with certainty that the reports were already prepared and typed out, or are you sure that the secretary typed out the reports that were made at that moment by those who had to report? So were reports already there? Can you exclude for that possibility or can you not exclude for that possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do believe that they hadn't been typed out in advance and composed; and for 99 per cent certainty, I can exclude that possibility because the information from my report was not something that the secretary could have come by until she had seen my report, until I had brought my report. Whether it was sent by fax to the commander, I don't know. You would have to ask him that. However, I'm quite convinced that nobody had the details and information until my report reached Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, do you recall when you wrote the report? This report writing took place in Zagreb, was it the same day that Mr. Turkalj issued the order, which was 1st September, or sometime after that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I don't want to give you the wrong information. But if the order was written on the 1st, then it could have been the 1st of September or the day after, depending on where they were, whether the people were in the field. After the field, they were either on furlough having free days or somewhere. And if he received the report, it is possible that not all the group leaders attended the meeting that day. Upon receiving the order, he called us all in. However, as I say, that could have been on the second day, because everybody attended the meeting. But perhaps the best thing would be to ask him because I don't want to say something that may not be quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do you know if -- as to whose report was typed first? Was it your report which was typed by the secretary first, before the group leaders; or were their reports typed before yours? Would you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I am convinced that it was my report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: You explain as to why you, in fact, back dated your report, because you said you merely followed your handwritten report. Now, Mr. Balunovic report is also back dated to 25th August. Do you know if anyone instructed the group leaders to back date their report? Mr. Celic, is the interpretation still proceeding? Because you're not responding to my question.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I'm listening to the interpreter. Now, as far as the date is concerned, nobody said what date should be put. Whether that is a mistake or not, I don't know. But since the event took place on the 25th, then the report should have been tabled the same day, and we placed that same date there. If the commander's report was on the 1st of September, maybe that should have been the date. But we didn't pay attention to that, nor did anybody tell us to back date. There was no discussion about that, nobody looked at that especially, or dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Registrar, may I have document P573, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Celic, you will see on the screen now an identical report as the one we just saw of Mr. Balunovic with an additional paragraph, just like your report, mentioning that the unit was instructed to comply with international humanitarian law. I think it's at the last -- yeah, the one before the last paragraph, before the list of names are indicated. Now, it seems that he, Mr. Balunovic, too, has submitted a second report with that additional paragraph. Now, I'm not going to go through all the group leaders report, and we have tendered into evidence two reports from each of the three group leaders; one without the paragraph, one with the paragraph. Now, was there some kind of consensus at that time that this paragraph should be inserted?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: While the group leaders were writing reports, everyone had his own office and everyone wrote in his own office. When we gave it to the typist to type it up, well, quite simply, you can see that the reports were coordinated in terms of those specific parts. Somebody had written something and somebody else had written something else. But if we're talking about what I wrote in my own report, it was good for it to be clued in the report because it was actually the truth. And that was conveyed to all the soldiers at the very beginning, that there were civilians and that it had to do with civilians. So this is something that was not mentioned in the report, but the content is true; and I believe that, at the time, the reports were coordinated at the secretary. Somebody had written something up, somebody else had not, and then when you see that they were not all the same, then these portions could be included.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could move on to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My first question is: Did you see this second report of Mr. Balunovic also in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: The first and the second were all written on the same day. I'm convinced that it was all written on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, on the face of it, the signature is different to the previous one. Do you know Mr. Balunovic to use this type of signature, or is it someone else placing his signature on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I'm convinced that this is his signature, but the best thing would be for you to ask him to have an expertise of the handwriting carried out. But I'm convinced that he is the one who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I asked it merely because you identified the previous signature also, which was different. The two names are written differently, and you said that certainly looks like his signature. That is why I asked you, Mr. Celic.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: In view of the fact that he was my subordinate, at that moment, I was assistant commander, and he was an instructor for specialised training; and during every assignment, every task, he was supposed to report to me, and I have quite a few of his reports. And I know that sometimes he signed his full name and surname and sometimes he just signed this way. So I am convinced that this report and the other one have his signature on them. I repeat that once again. But perhaps the best thing would have to have an expertise carried out, and then he could give his views on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document P568, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And while that is being brought up, Mr. Celic, did you see the reports of the other two group leaders, too; that is, Mr. Zinic and Mr. Krajina's reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I did see all the reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And are you aware that the two of them, too, submitted a second report with that additional paragraph? Did you see that second report of theirs?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you ask this Mr. Zinic -- Mr. Zinic, as to the veracity or the truthfulness of this report, why he was now submit ago different report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I shall repeat once again. From that meeting that I talked about, at that moment, he and Mr. Balunovic did not know that anything had happened. But on the basis of my report, they wrote the other reports. Everybody had to state their views because it was obvious that something had happened, but I'm convinced he did not know at that time what it was that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And was it the case for Mr. Krajina, too, the group leader? I could actually have that -- his report brought up.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness would answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just wanted to show him the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for Branko Balunovic and Stjepan Licnik [phoen], they had the left flank of the search, in accordance with my orders. So, I'm convinced that since Grubori is in the middle or rather, on the right side, I believe that they could not have been at that position. That is why I believe what they said; that is to say, two group leaders were on the right-hand side, one of them was Mr. Krajina. Now, whether he did see something or did not see something, I cannot say because he had also told me nothing had happened. But the report says something different.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could bring up document 570, please, P.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you have a discussion with Mr. Krajina in Zagreb at the time that you were citing these reports?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: At that meeting, we all took part in the discussion, and Mr. Krajina also did not know that anything had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, so, did you ask -- can you tell us, do you know what the basis of Mr. Krajina's report is, which is on the screen right now? I'm sorry. Before that, let me ask you a question. Did you see there report in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes. This is Mr. Krajina's report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you ask him why he was submitting this version of events; or is it the same for him, too, that he was following your report?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I think that the best thing would be for you to ask him that, but I will try to explain it from my point of view. He was also on the right-hand side and that happened where he was. He also stated that nothing had happened at the initial position, and it is undeniable that this was in his area and he was to report on that, as we have all seen. Now, whether he did see that something happened or not, whether these officers were from his group, I really can't say, I don't know. But the event itself took place in his area, and I believe that that is why he wrote this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And based on your experience, if, in fact, there was an actual armed resistance in this area, was there any reason for any of these group leaders not to report that fact to you? Do you see any reason?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: On the contrary, it would be their duty to report, so that we would resolve the situation in the best possible way. It was their duty to report on anything, had anything been happening in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: While you were waiting for these units, did you hear any noises or sound or some indications that would have indicated to you that there was, in fact, an armed resistance or some form of conflict taking place in the area; explosions, continuous gun-fire, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: If I knew how to put this event into a context of time, I could give you a far more accurate answer. However, I said in my statement that I went out and I came back because I came across civilians; and, together with Commander Janic, I got into the car and we went to the other position that is quite far away from this position.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my question was: Did you hear? That's only my question. Was there any indication to you while you were waiting either at the start position or at the end that there was some form of armed conflict taking place in the area? I'm talking about explosions, continuous gun-fire. Was there any such evidence?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Not explosions, but occasional gun-fire was heard. I wanted to explain another thing to you. If there was an explosion, since this is a hill that it pretty high, and perhaps at that moment I was on the other side of the hill, there is the possibility of not hearing the explosion. But while I was there, I did not hear any explosions. However, gun-fire was heard, either from a rifle or a gun, but the gun-fire had nothing to do with any kind of combat, open fire. It was occasional gun-fire, in order to have a lineup or whatever else. I personally also fired a bullet from my rifle, in order to signal to the driver to come to my position. So you could hear shots every now and then; but that there was a large-scale conflict or you could hear explosions, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: The gun-fire that you heard, the occasional gun-fire, was it in that -- in the context that you were such that would not alert you that there was some form of armed clash was going on, or was it the kind of gun-fire in that context you were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Mahindaratne. Has that question not been answered already by the previous answers?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Celic, your evidence was that of the four group leaders, three submitted reports; but Mr. Drljo, the fourth leader - pardon my pronunciation if I did not pronounce that name right - refused to submit a report. And if could I take to you to your 2002 statement, that's part 3 of 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It's page 11; in the filed version, it is page 13775.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And if I could read -- a question is put to you: "I just want to clarify this point. After your three men were asked to submit reports your four -- actually, four group leaders, and Franjo Drljo refused, who did you actually personally report his failure to submit a report to?" And your response is: "All of them, and to my commander. I said that to my commander, Mr. Turkalj, and he informed Mr. Markac and Sacic. So they knew about it." Next question is: "But were you present when he actually -- did you actually witness him telling Sacic and Markac?" Your responses: "I believe they knew that; and, again, the day when I wrote the report I believe that he was called. I believe, again, I don't know who was present at the meeting, but I believe they knew. They called Franjo Drljo and they talked to him, because I had to write the report that day. The others had to write it later." Now, first and foremost, you refer to Franjo Drljo being called on a day that you had to write a report. Which day are you referring to? Because you wrote reports on two days, on 26th and Mr. Sacic dictated, and then later on, pursuant to Mr. Turkalj's order. Which day was Mr. Drljo called?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Mr. Drljo was called in when we were all in Zagreb and when we wrote our reports in Zagreb. My first report, on the 26th, well, I was the only one who was there and Mr. Sacic. No one was there, no one else. And I believe that the unit was already on its way to Zagreb, on the basis of a written order that was issued by Mr. Turkalj then. We were all present at that meeting, I and the four group leaders. And that is when we were all told that we all had to submit reports in Zagreb, and I believe that that was on the 1st of September, but I don't want to give you any kind of misinformation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you say that you believe that Mr. Turkalj informed Mr. Markac and Sacic of Mr. Drljo's failure to submit a report. Now, what's the basis for that response? What makes you think that Mr. Turkalj telephoned Mr. Markac or Sacic? Do you know that for a fact, were you there, or did Mr. Turkalj inform you?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: At that meeting, Mr. Turkalj, the then-commander, read out the written report that he had received -- or rather, he issued a written order to us. And on the basis of this written order, he was duty-bound to submit reports and a response, and I am convinced that he had to write something in that report of his that he had to submit to the sector. It was his duty to inform the sector, to send all our reports. If someone had not done that, then he would have to write why that had happened. That was his duty, and that is how I believed that he had no inform the sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you say that "they called," you refer to somebody calling Franjo Drljo. You said: "They called Franjo Drljo and they talked to him." Whom do you refer to as "they"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether somebody had called him or not; but probably, if someone was supposed to call him, it should have been the commander. I cannot say. I would be wrong if I would say that it was Mr. Sacic or Mr. Markac. I guess that I would misspeak. I really do not know. What I know are the facts. On that day, he was called by Mr. Turkalj, like all of us, and that is when he knew this. Now, whether anybody discussed that with him, apart from the commander, that I really cannot say. I don't know. I can just make assumptions, but I'm not sure. Quite simply, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I have document 625, please, P625.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, in the meanwhile, if could you look at your interview of 2002, section 2, page 30 going on 31. Actually, in your section, in your version, B/C/S, it's page 28 to 29.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: In the filed version, it is page 13800.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you have been questioned, Mr. Celic, about the fire-arms that your unit was carrying in the course of the Oluja-Obruc operation on 25th and 26, and you say this: "The short weapons that you call the pistol and the long weapons; and the long ones, they were different types of rifles."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could we be advised of the more specific details relating to this document. I mean, who is issuing the document, when was this document issued. We have -- we have no indication on that topic on the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this moment, I think what Ms. Mahindaratne was doing was she was just quoting for the witness his statement; and then, of course, we except her to add a question to that. Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm citing of your interview records. Then you describe the weapons that -- that your unit had, and you say: "Automatic rifles from the former JNA." And you were asked a question: "Did you have any form of support in the way of artillery or anything like that? "No. "Did you have any weapons shall we say for launching grenades? "No, we didn't. For that type of operation, we didn't have that. "So the only weapons that your men carried were handguns, like pistols, resolvers, and rifles, and then you say hand-grenades. "Again, I cannot say exactly who was carrying what type of weapons, for example, if somebody had a sniper rifle. But from the heavy artillery like mortars, we didn't have that." Before getting to the document, I also want to show you another part and ask you the question, Mr. Celic. If I could take to you to your 2005 interview notes, to section -- to part 2 of 2005.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's 5275, page 14 to 15. In the filed version, it is page 13523.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, there, you were asked: "Mr. Ceric, you said you had a Motorola for communication. On this particular day, was there a necessity for your men to take, should we say, the anti-tank armoury with them, you know, the weapons we discussed earlier?" And you say: "Nobody carried it, as far as I know." Now, my question is: Were the weapons that were carried by the unit recorded; as in, were weapons issued to the individual members of the unit recorded somewhere?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: As for weapons, all members of the unit were issued with basic weapons, long barrelled or short barrelled, a gun, a pistol, and a rifle. You asked me about automatic weapons. There are different types: The automatic rifle used by the former JNA, their rifles; Ultimax; SAR; FAR [phoen]; Heckler. All of that was recorded in the personal files of the soldier. When going out into the field, if a soldier has two or three rifles, he could take any one of them. It was not particularly pointed out what it was that he had to take. Those are basic weapons. There are also specialised weapons. Officers belong to different groups. You mentioned sniper shooters within a unit. Where there were 100 or 120 men, there were ten men who were sniper shooters. There was the possibility for a soldier not to take an automatic rifle, but, rather, a sniper rifle, because he had also been issued with one of those. No one stopped them from doing any kind of thing. As for anti-armour weapons --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my question. The first question was: Were - and then you answer it - all weapons issued to the personnel of the unit recorded? Is there a record of the weapons issued to the personnel?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: As for weapons, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And weapons such as anti-tank weapons, any hand-held rocket launchers, that type of weapons, how were they issued? Were they issued to the individual members or as a unit in general?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Only to individuals in the unit. As for anti-armour weapons, when you're talking about hand-held rocket launchers, not everyone could have those. I will explain. They are RPGs, and they're not supposed to be used only once. So a soldier would be issued with that weapon and that was recorded in the files and everyone knew, but then there were also Zoljas that were supposed to be used only once. That was not included in the personal files of the soldiers concerned. If there was a particular action involved, if the security assessment was that there would be anti-armour combat, then the soldiers could take these weapons, specifically Zoljas, one or two, take them out into the field. But these weapons were not included in the said person's personal file.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you have any information that during the operation on 25th and 26th, the Oluja-Obruc operation, that you would face anti-armour combat? Was there any such report to that nature in advance of the operation?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: As for the strength, I cannot say exactly. This is to say that we had received information that, perhaps, in this area, there were some terrorist groups that were still left behind, because in the immediate vicinity, there was fighting going on. So there was the possibility of someone being there, someone having stayed behind. I cannot say how strong these terrorist groups were exactly. However, in view of the terrain, of course, we did not except any kind of heavy weaponry to be there, or something like that. Personnel was expected, if any.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, to your knowledge, do you know if the weapons that you described as Zoljas or anti-tank weapons -- you have already said they were not -- were there not, but were Zoljas carried around on 25th and 26th?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Never going out into the field. Soldiers were issued orders as to what kind of weapons they were supposed to bring along. They knew that they had to have long barrelled and short barrelled weapons, absolutely. Now, in Operation Storm or from earlier on, a soldier could have had a Zolja. No one could have stopped anyone from carrying a Zolja, but this was not pointed out, that any kind of anti-armour weapons were supposed to be taken along. Since people were psychologically and physically fit and prepared, this was no problem for them to carry a lot of gear. Now, whether people actually did, I really cannot say; however, it was not said to them specifically that they should. I believe that probably some of the men did carry such weapons, because in terms of tactics, and not only for anti-armour combat, if the enemy has a fortified position, then anti-armour projectiles can be used. I'm convinced that someone must have had something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you see, as far as you're concerned, did you see members of the unit carrying Zoljas, either on the 25th or the 26th?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I don't want to say anything that is wrong, but the line was long at the initial position. And before going out into the field, people did not take weapons and come to see me; rather, before going out, they would go to their vehicles, they would take all their equipment and go out into the field. I personally did not see this personally, but there is such a possibility. I personally did not see this, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And I do not in you answered this, Mr. Celic. If Zoljas are issued, are they issued to the members individually or as a unit?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Not individually. During the previous actions, he could have -- anybody could have picked up a Zolja.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So, if Zolja has been issued to the unit, that would be on record somewhere, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Well, let me give you an example from Operation Storm, Action Storm itself. When we set out to the action, we came out onto the road the next day, and it was our task to take control of that communication line. Now, before we reached that position -- or before we reach a position, we don't know whether we will have to engage in fighting, whether there will be fire or not. So people do take a certain amount of ammunition, as much as they can carry, in fact. So, at that position, where with certainty our vehicles and logistics can reach us, as we were brought water and food, they also bring us ammunition. So, quite possibility, people use up the ammunition, and Zoljas are brought in a van, too. So we could have had ammunition and we could have the Zoljas, too. So, if somebody needed a more of anything, they could take it, and there wasn't any separate record kept about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Celic, do you recognise the document on this screen?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: No. I do -- I am familiar with the information there, but not the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you not have to submit lists of the weapons that the Lucko Unit carried on 25th August 1995 to Mr. Janic, in the course of the subsequent investigations that were conducted into the Grubori event?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I don't remember this document. I can't say that I've seen it. I think that we had to supply documents, and the information is clear to me, the names and the surnames and all that; but I can't say just off the top of my head whether Stepjan -- well, was issued such-and-such. I do know the names, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't asking you for details. I was trying to figure out if you would be familiar with the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could go into the next few pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, if you could just take a look at this document and let us know if you have any familiarity with this document.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Specifically, as far as my name and surname is concerned, everything that it says here is absolutely correct. Those are the weapons that I was issued. Now, of course, I can't say with any certainty about anybody else who had what weaponry. But when it comes to my name and me personally, I can confirm that the information there is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Do you remember at any stage in 2004, 2003, or 2005, were you asked by Mr. Janic to submit or to compile a list of the weapons and details of the personnel who were involved in the 26th August operation, on 25th, in the Plavno area. Do you recall submitting a list to Mr. Janic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Well, I really can't answer that. I think that when the investigation started, that details were called for, where asked. Now, who had what, I don't think that we could have known that, so I can't really answer that question. I think they asked for details from the entire unit, who was issued what; but whether on that day anything specific was asked for, as to who was there and what rifle, I really can't tell you more about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, no. You misunderstood my question, Mr. Celic. My question is: Were you, at some stage in 2004 or 2005, requested by Mr. Janic to compile a list of the personnel of the Lucko Unit, what weapons were issued to them, et cetera? Were you asked by Mr. Janic, in 2004, to compile a list of the list -- the men who were attached to the Lucko Unit and the weapons issued to them? That's my question, not as to whether you knew what they really carried on 25th August.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes. I understood you to ask with about the action, but I do believe that when the investigation started, he did ask for this report and that it was submitted, but I am not 100 percent sure. I do believe it was, though, for the entire unit, not for the day, but what all the people were issued. So my answer is, I do believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I'm looking at the clock. It is approximately the time where we usually have a break. I don't know whether you are --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break, and we'll resume at a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for the witness to come into the courtroom, I already inquire with the parties about the scheduling, not because as to often put a bit of pressure, but rather to know whether the next witness should remain available. Ms. Mahindaratne, could you give us an indication.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I believe I might take my full four hours, Mr. President, but I have already cut down a lot in the course of the break, so it is possible that I could finish before the end of the day. If that happens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the witness will be cross-examined on from that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the other parties give me any indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course, it depends on the further direct

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Other Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Nothing arises, Your Honour, for us, at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Nothing for us either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That means that there's a fair chance that we'll finish tomorrow by somewhere during the second session. This might be information which is relevant for the next witness in line. Ms. Mahindaratne, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, may I call for document number 1857, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, your testimony was that a few days after the operation, Mr. Turkalj ordered you to go to Grubori accompanied by Mr. Balunovic, and Mr. Turkalj also went with you. Then you further said that when you went to Grubori on that occasion, you saw three bodies and a few burnt houses, and you could not remember exactly when you went to Grubori. Now, in the course of the interview, you were shown this document. Can you recognise this document? Now, this is a report from Mr. Dondo to Mr. Cermak, and I think you saw this in the course of the interview and talked about what you could offer about this.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I was shown this during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's correct. My question is this: Now, in this report, Mr. Dondo reports that of 25 houses, some 20 houses and many farm buildings set ablaze, and five bodies were recovered. This is dated 26th August. It further records that the bodies would be removed on 27th August. Now, your testimony was that when you went to Grubori, you saw three bodies. I'm just trying to get at the date that you went to Grubori, Mr. Celic. Now, if, in fact, it was correct that bodies were removed on the 27th, considering that you saw the bodies, could it be that you visited Grubori on the 27th August? Is that a possibility? Are you able to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: With respect to what you just said, yes, absolutely, that possibility does exist. On the 25th, we had a search of the terrain there, and then on the 26th in a second area, then we went to Zagreb. So the possibility does exist that that was the 27th. Yes, I do believe that was what it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And the other fact I wanted to point out in this report is, now, in this report, Mr. Dondo reports to Mr. Cermak that of 25 houses, 20 houses were set ablaze. Your testimony was that you saw only a few houses. Can you explain that? How is it that you did not see the other houses that were set ablaze?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I didn't say that they were burning, but that that they had been set ablaze. Now, as the configuration of the hamlet is such, you don't have a classical form of street where one house backs straight to another. They are all scattered houses, and the terrain is slightly hilly. So, on the route that I passed, I just saw a few. I didn't go all over the area. And from the position that I was in, I couldn't see that all the houses were burning; but where I did pass by, I saw some. I don't know that there were 25 houses set ablaze. If there were, I did not see them because I didn't pass by that whole area.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: When you say "the whole area," did you walk around the whole village of Grubori? That's my question. When you say "area," are you referring to the village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: No, I'm not referring to the village. I just passed by a few houses, and it's a hamlet. There were a few houses on one side and a few on the other. I don't know where the village starts and how many houses the village has. But just on the road that I went, that was probably Grubori, and I'm quite convinced I didn't go through the whole village, only that area where this happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to move this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P764, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P764 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Celic, your testimony was that when you went to Grubori on this day, that you saw three bodies. You also saw Mr. Cermak in Grubori with other people, you say, from his office and an HTV crew, and you saw Mr. Cermak being interviewed by the HTV crew. You also said that prior to going to Grubori, you were informed that Mr. Cermak would be there in Grubori on the day you went. Now, who gave that you information?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I think it was Mr. Turkalj.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, did you hear what Mr. Cermak was telling the TV crew? Did you catch perhaps excerpts of that interview?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: No, I did not. I knew Mr. Cermak before that personally. I went up to him, said hello; but what he actually said, I couldn't hear because I wasn't nearby when the interview was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And did you see Mr. Cermak walking around in the village, perhaps going through that area where there were burnt houses, or where the bodies were?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: We all went together. It was a group of people. I can't tell you how many of us there were exactly, but we were a group. Mr. Cermak was there, I was there, Commander Turkalj was there, and people from the Cermak security, and I assume we went past that way together. And when we passed, we saw what happened; but I was in the group together with my commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in the course of, you know, walking around, did you hear Mr. Cermak discuss anything about the Grubori incident with Mr. Turkalj or any other person present in the group, or perhaps yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: While we were passing -- well, there's a small path through the hamlet and we couldn't all be at the same time because it was a narrow path, and we went by in a column of seven to ten metres, one behind the other. And as far as that event goes, I remember that I was with Commander Turkalj all the time, and we were looking to see what had happened. We passed by the houses to see where the bodies were, and so on, and where the houses were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony, you also say that you saw civilians speaking to the TV crew and, you believe, with Mr. Cermak. Did you -- my question is: Did you see the civilians speaking to him, or are you not certain about it? Was that a guess? Because you said "I believe they spoke with Mr. Cermak." That is what your testimony is.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I will try and depict the facts as I know them. It was a small village, a hamlet; you could see the path; you could see civilians, I can't say how many of them there were. But there were some elderly women, and it was they, in fact, who indicated to us where this had happened. And since we were going along in a column, I couldn't really say what they were talking to -- what they were talking about with the TV crew and with Mr. Cermak. But I know that there were civilians, and we were shown the bodies and where the houses were, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you said that after that visit, you went to Knin to Mr. Cermak's office and had lunch there, and you say that Mr. Sacic also was present. Did you see Mr. Sacic and Mr. Cermak discuss or have a -- talk to each other?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: During the investigation itself, I couldn't determine the time, whether can he wept to Knin before or after, I assume it was afterwards. So, at the meeting, there was myself, Mr. Turkalj, Mr. Cermak, and Mr. Sacic, and the event was discussed. All of us discussed it. All of us were in one room and discussed what had had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you said this was Mr. Cermak's office. How do you know it was Mr. Cermak's office?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Well, since there were soldiers there; and since I know that the headquarters was in Gracac and not Knin, Knin was closer to this place than Gracac was. So it was logical that we went there, and that's where the army was, the police -- or the military, rather. I know that the police weren't there and that's why I was convinced that it was Mr. Cermak's office, and I hope that that is, indeed, the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And when you said you had a discussion, you said, Mr. Turkalj, Mr. Cermak, Mr. Sacic, and yourself, you all talked about the incident. Did you, at that meeting, talk about the fact that, you know, after the incident, none of the group leaders had reported to you anything? Did you recount what you have told us at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Precisely. I do believe that that is the case. I didn't have anything to say with respect to the event itself. Mr. Sacic and Mr. Turkalj knew that, and Mr. Balunovic knew that. Mr. Cermak could not have known that. But I said on the occasion that, quite simply, I didn't know what had happened. Quite the contrary, I knew that nothing had happened, so I couldn't talk about it really. I was asked to say what had happened, but I said that according to what I knew, nothing had happened; whereas, Mr. Sacic knew something more judging by what he said. That's what I wrote; whereas, in actual fact, I did not know of that event.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Balunovic was also at this meeting, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I do believe he was because we were together all the time, so I do believe that he was there, too. Mr. Turkalj was there for sure, I was there for sure, Mr. Sacic was there fur sure, and I do believe that Mr. Balunovic was there, too, because there was a quite a lot of people there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Cermak there? Because you're talking about the meeting in Mr. Cermak's office when you went down to lunch there.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did anybody, Mr. Cermak or Mr. Sacic or Mr. Turkalj, talk - or Mr. Balunovic since he was group leader who would have been in that area - about the incident at that meeting; or did Mr. Balunovic tell them about what he could offer about the incident at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Well, I do believe that all of us spoke and that we discussed it with him, too. But I'd also like to repeat and say that I don't believe that at that point in time that he knew that anything had happened, just like me. I didn't know, I couldn't describe the event. All I could say is that the group leaders had told me no nothing had happened. That's all I could have said, and I think that is the same thing that he could have said. Now, whether he said something more than that, I really can't say, I don't know. Perhaps you should look at his statement and see for yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, the expression "nothing had happened" is heard many, many times. I do understand that we're talking about a lunch after a joint visit to Grubori. Could you please, in your line of questioning, include several possible events: The first one being whether there had any combat or like activity. Of course, the witness testified already what he knows about that; the second, about the houses set ablaze in Grubori; and the third, that civilians were found dead in Grubori. Because if I read an answer, "All could I say is that the group leaders had told me nothing had happened," that, of course, apparently refers to reporting, but not the actual knowledge of the witness after he had been to Grubori. So could we always clearly distinguish between these several elements, and also distinguish between what time, what was said, and what we have to assume on the basis of the evidence given by this witness was known at the time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Celic, this lunch in Mr. Cermak's office, this took place after you, Mr. Turkalj, and Mr. Balunovic have -- had already visited Grubori and you saw those bodies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I think it is. Now, I wasn't able to be precise in my statement. As to time, I had my doubts as to whether it was before or after the visit to Grubori. So I couldn't says whether it was before or after, but I do believe that it was afterwards; that is to say, that the visit came first and that we went over there later on. That's how I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, do you remember going to the Grubori in the morning or in the evening? When you saw these bodies, was it morning?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: It was all during the day because I know that pursuant to orders on that day - and if we're talking about the 27th and I do believe we are - then we had to be in Gracac at 7.00 in the morning. So Mr. Balunovic and I arrived in Gracac at 7.00 a.m.; and I assume that from Gracac, we went to Grubori straight away; and then, afterwards, to Knin. That's what I think happened. But it was daylight throughout. It was day when we arrived in Gracac, when we were in Grubori, and when we were in Knin. It was day throughout, during the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And how long does it take to go to Grubori from Gracac, time-wise?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, perhaps an hour to hour and a half. It depends when you move off the main road. You have to drive slowly. So it might take one to one and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So when you met at Mr. Cermak's office for lunch that day, you had already -- I mean, is it the case that you already had seen the bodies and the burnt houses?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: When I was in Grubori, I saw the bodies and the houses, but let me try and be precise. I think that if you look at other reports, you will be able to define whether that was before or after the meeting. I believe that we went to Grubori first; and, of course, saw the bodies and houses there. That is what I think, and that we went to Knin afterwards. That's what I think happened, but I leave the possibility that we might have gone to Knin first. I can't be absolutely sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, you kept saying that whenever certain questions were asked, you said: "I could say only what I knew, which was that nothing happened." Now, when you said "that nothing happened," were you referring to what was reported to you at the end of the operation on the 25th? Is that what you're referring to? Because you knew at some stage that there were civilians killed and houses set on fire, so what did you mean when you said "nothing happened"?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: What I was asked to do is this: To say what we had seen and to say what I knew about that, and I said that the only thing that I was this: That the group leaders were duty-bound to report to me, to inform me of an armed resistance, of a conflict, that there had been firing, or anything that might have happened in the field. They should have informed me straight away; if they couldn't have reached me, then at the final line. So my information at that time was that everything went well, that there was no combat, that there wasn't a armed conflict, no firing, which means that nothing had actually happened. Now, after the Grubori visit, and I think that after we had been to Knin, I was asked to say what I knew about it, because my unit went past that way, so it was my duty to know what had happened in the area. But I said at the time that I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: So when you say "nothing happened," what you're referring to is the reports you referred -- the reports you received from the group leaders at the end of the operation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: That's right. It was oral reporting, not a written report. The reports were made to me by the group leaders orally, oral reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, at this lunch, did Mr. Cermak ask you, If that is the case, how is that there are civilians killed, houses burnt? How is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object now at this stage because I've lead a lot of the leading go, and I think it would be more appropriate if Ms. Mahindaratne actually asked, What did Mr. Cermak say, not actually put it to the witness in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. I will rephrase. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, do you recall what Mr. Cermak asked you about this incident? Did he ask you anything?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Well, the conversation went like this: Mr. Sacic spoke mostly, and he was the highest ranked person there. Now, specifically, I cannot claim whether Mr. Cermak asked me whether such-and-such had happened and whether I know such-and-such, whether I know what happened, because it was Mr. Sacic that did most of the talking.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do you recall if Mr. Cermak asked Mr. Sacic anything?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to give you the wrong information. The event was discussed, everything was discussed. There was a lot of us in that room, and I'm sure you have the information and details about what was discussed. Because if I were to tell you now, I might make a mistake. All I can say is that in general terms, we discussed the event, what had happened, when it happened, what unit had passed by that way. I couldn't say for sure, because I had received a report that nothing had happened, so I couldn't really discuss the matter much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Let me move on, Mr. Celic, to the operation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I'd like to ask the witness to tell us what Mr. Sacic, who, as you told us, was speaking most being of a higher rank, what did he explain or what did he tell about when you said about what had happened? But what did he say about any combat during the 25th, about the houses apparently set ablaze, and about the civilians that were dead? What did he tell at that meeting about these three subjects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in view of the time that's passed by, I wouldn't want to quote exactly what he said, but I believe that he spoke in the context of the report that I had written -- or rather, that he had told me to write. And I imagine that he explained what had had happened within that context, but I cannot say decidedly now that he said such-and-such a thing. I mean, I really couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what he explained was roughly in accordance with what he had dictated to you write in your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that that is exactly the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When having lunch, were you sitting at one table or how were you positioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could not say for sure whether lunch was before this meeting or afterwards. I think it was afterwards. It was a biggish room, there were separate tables. I think that they were all in that room, but I don't know how it was that we were sitting exactly. I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You make a distinction now between the meeting and lunch. That meeting, how were you seated, how was this organised? Were you sitting around a table, were you standing, was there one person in front of the others? Explaining what actually happened, how was that meeting organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am making a distinction because we had the meeting before lunch, not during lunch. There was this room; and in addition to the people from the special police that I have already mentioned, there were some from the military, some from the police. I don't know exactly how many were there. There were quite a few people there. We were in this one room. I don't know if the table was a round table; but at any rate, we could all see each other, and that is what was discussed. Right now, I could not give the exact seating arrangement, and I could not tell you what the room looked like. Definitely, it wasn't over lunch. We had the meeting, and then we went to lunch. I think it was after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How do I have to understand that meeting to take place? Was it one person speaking, the others listening, and then another person speaking, and then the others listening; or was it a kind of a structured discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is what I could say: Since it had to do with us - that is to say, our unit, my unit - we were asked -- I mean, well, to say what it was that had actually happened. I believe that Mr. Sacic did most of the talking about this because he knew the most about this. I don't know what you mean, how this was structured. Quite simply, what was required was to see what had happened and Mr. Sacic had the most to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do I then understand that he addressed the others who were present and said so that everyone could hear his words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm convinced that the answer is yes, because it was one single room, unless he spoke to someone sitting right next to him at a particular point in time; but, otherwise, absolutely you could hear everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you sitting next to him, or were you sitting at a distance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were all in a single room. I did not sit right next to him. Perhaps I was a few metres away. It wasn't very far away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Please proceed, Ms. Mahindaratne.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, I will move on to the operation the day after 26th. But before that, let me just show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could call -- it's 65 ter number 5398.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, your testimony was that before you started the operation on 25th, you were advised that there would be civilians in the area. Do you recognise this document by any chance, or do you know who compiled this document?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of this document, and I don't know who compiled it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I move to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do we have any specific on that document?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, but we do -- I could include it into a bar table motion. At this stage, I don't have it. This is document that we have received from -- in response to RFA from the Croatian government, as one of the documents collected in the course of the Grubori investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. But do we know when this document was typed or written or who write it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: No. That is what I was trying find out from the witness. It can be connected to another list which has already been admitted into evidence, a list civilians found in the Plavno area on the 25th, which is a much larger list. And this is it part of that list. You know, at least the names are contained in that other list, which is already in evidence. This is it relevant because of a matter that was raised by the Cermak Defence, as to the origins of that list of civilians, which is why I have tendered this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. Since we don't know who the author is, since we don't when document has been produced, I certainly object to the admissibility of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other list, Ms. Mahindaratne, would be?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this stage, I don't have that list. May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You referred to that and you say this list is more or less an extract, apparently a handwritten extract; and then, of course, I would, in order to get a proper understanding of what you tell us, I'd like to look at that other list, or the Chamber might want to look at that other list as well, to see how it was introduced, what we know about the other list, be able to compare whether this list really is an extract or whether it is different, whether the other list was handwritten as well. Well, a lot of questions, but then we have to know what the other list --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: If you could give me just a couple of minutes, Mr. President, I'll give it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have it marked for identification. I take it that the Chamber will not take a decision anyhow, immediately. Mr. Registrar, could is a number be assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P765, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I take it that you will provide with us the relevant information as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, may I call document P580, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, I'd like to you look at your 2002 statement, and that's P761, part -- third part, page 39.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S version, it's page 38; in the filed version, it's 13747.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: There's a discussion about the operation on 26th August; and at page 39, right at the bottom in the English version, you say -- you refer to that operation and you say: "The group went through the village. I don't know how and in which way because I was in a lower point than the village was, but it was seen that the houses were on fire." Going on to page 40: "At which point, I was called by General Markac whom, after the search, I also again, at the end point, I had been waiting for." And you say: "Again, my group leaders or commanders of the groups also reported to me that there was no contact, any contact whatsoever with anybody." Now, this is a reference to the operation on the 26th, in the Promina area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And do you recognise the document on the -- I appreciate you may not have seen the document, but isn't this operation that Mr. Markac has informed the Split Military District and Knin -- it is referred to as forward command post. Isn't this the operation that was conducted in the Promina area? This is what you have spoken to about in the course of the interview.

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I have never seen this report, I mean this piece of information; however, according to the information concerned in the area where we were, on the 26th, well, on the basis of our report -- or rather, my report from that day, you can see exactly what the positions were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to point out. Now, in this report of Mr. Markac, there's a reference to a village called Ramljane. Pardon my pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: It is R-a-m-l-j-a-n-e, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, at the interview, you have been referring to houses being set on fire in a particular village. Is that the village you're referring to, Ramljane?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I think it was. But if you have my report, you will be able to see exactly whether that it is. On the basis of my recollection, I would say that that's it, but, then, you do have my report. That is where I refer to all the tasks and locations, and you will be able to see from there; however, I believe that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, were the group leaders in this operation also the same four group leaders as on 25th August?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I think so, or perhaps I subdivided the unit into two groups there view of the terrain, but I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And you say that you were at a lower point than the village was, but you could see that the houses were on fire. Now, was it the case that, just like on 25th, you did not accompany the unit on its axis; or can you explain exactly what happened, with regard to yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: When carrying out such tasks, it wasn't my duty to go out with the men. My duty was to be the coordinator between the unit and other units; that is to say, I take care of my unit. I have group leaders who are supposed to report their positions to me, if there's an armed conflict, and I convey that further. At that point in time, I'm not duty-bound to with be the unit, although did I go on the first day. When I gave specific orders to the group leaders, when I sent them out into the field from the initial position, then I went to the ending point. That is to say, that it was not my duty to go out in the field with the many; on the contrary, I was supposed to be the coordinator for the unit. And that's where I stayed there in this last position after they were sent out, and then I went to the point where their task was supposed to end.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What did you mean by: "I did go on the first day." When you say "the first day," what are you referring to? Was it the 25th August operation that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Precisely, precisely. You can see that from the report that I set out with the unit, and then I returned. Since I came across civilians, you see that I went with the unit. On the second day, I did not go, and I wanted to explain that, that it was not my duty to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, on this day also, was the overall operations commander Mr. Janic?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And can you explain, when you saw that you were at a lower point than the village but it was seen that the houses were on fire, now was this right at the beginning of the operation or after a little while the unit had already moved on? After how long the operation started did you see the houses were on fire?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer with any certainty. On the road between Knin and Drnis, you actually turn right from that road in order to reach the localities that we're discussing, and then you climb up into the hills. When you go back to the main road, you cannot see -- or rather, you cannot see the houses. However, you can see smoke far away. So if the smoke goes very high, then you can see it. So, at first, when I was at the position, I did not see anything on fire. After leaving that position, it was obvious that houses were on fire. I could not say exactly say what time this was; but, certainly, after some time, after the soldiers [as interpreted] set out to carry out their task.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, between the time the soldiers had moved on and the time you saw the smoke, did you hear any gun-fire or explosions?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes, it could be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. It is the matter of correction translations. I see in the transcript that the word which witness used was translated as "soldiers"; and, afterwards, Ms. Mahindaratne repeated this word, but this is not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We could ask the witness what was the real word, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... ask the witness to repeat what he said. Could I ask you to again fill in part of your answer, which I will read to you. You said: "I could not say exactly what time this was; but, certainly, after some time, after the," and then that is the part to fill in, "had set out ..." --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that what you were looking for, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Mahindaratne, could you refer to "members of the unit."

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you don't have to apologise. I mean, it is not your fault that you took it from the transcript. So, perhaps, you repeat the question, starting on page 88, line 1, with the adapted language.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Mr. Celic, let me repeat my question. Now, from the time the members of the Lucko Unit moved on the operation and to the time that you started seeing the smoke rising, did you hear gun-fire?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Yes, it could be heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And what type of -- I mean, is it the way -- now you describe on 25th what you heard was sporadic gun-fire, but was this sporadic gun-fire or was this continuous gun-fire which may have indicated to you that there was combat activity?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: You just mentioned the 25th. I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... in relation --

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: This operation was on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I said in relation to the 25th operation, you said when you heard gun-fire it was sporadic. I said, likewise, on the 26th, the gun-fire that you heard, was it just sporadic gun-fire, once in a while; or was there continuous gun-fire which may indicate -- which may have indicated to you that there was combat activity?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of what was heard and what was seen, one could conclude that there had been contact. It wasn't a single firing of a rifle by way of a signal. You could hear the kind of gun-fire that meant that there was some kind of contact.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Did you hear explosions?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to give you any kind of wrong information; but, yes, yes, gun-fire was heard. I believe that there was an explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And, I certainly wouldn't know what a Zolja sounds like if you fired one, but could you hear from where you were whether there was Zoljas being fired?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't state that specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Celic, you tell me -- actually, you have told us in the interview that at the end of the operation, your group leaders reported to you that there was no contact and any contact whatsoever with anybody. Your language is: "My group leaders or commanders of the group also reported to me that there was no contact, any contact whatsoever with anybody." Now, did you ask them, If there was no contact, what was that gun-fire I heard; or did you inquire from them what the sounds were all about?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: When we are talking contact, we are talking about combat contact. In view of the fact that it was heard and seen, that houses were on fire, it was obvious that this had been contact. There is a report by Mr. Janic, and then he said that he would come and that General Markac would come; and we were all waiting for him there at the line, at ending line where we were supposed to report on combat contact because this was in the immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: My question is not about what you saw in terms of the houses on fire. But your group leaders, as you told us, came to you and said that nothing had happened. Now, what you say is you heard this noise, you heard gun-fire, which indicated to you that will there might have been combat activity. Now, did you ask them, If, in fact, nothing had happened, what was that gun-fire all about? Did you ask them what it was?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: At the last line, since I did not go with them, I took a different route, we all met up eventually. I met up with the members of the unit and Janic and General Markac and Mr. Sacic. When we met up there, then we discussed what had happened. It was my duty to report to the General there on the task that we had, where we had passed, and what had happened. In that report, I explained what group took what direction, who had what task. And what was specifically stated there was who went in what direction and also where the houses were and what had happened and one group leader had passed that way. After that was located, when I said which group leader had gone that way, General Markac talked to him so that he would tell him what it was had happened and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: And that group leader was Mr. Drljo. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: Now, if you could look at your 2002 interview notes, and section 3, page 14 in the English translation; B/C/S 39.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's the filed version 13746.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: That's the page we were at earlier on, and you go on to describe that operation. You say: "So we are going back to the start point where we are meeting General Markac, who told to us wait for him. On that occasion, I submitted to him my report where the search took place, and he wanted -- he personally requested to be told who was there; to which I told him that in that area in question where the houses were burned or set on fire was the group of Franjo Drljo, commander; to which he spoke to him and was asking him what was his direction of movement. "However, he was saying that he went around the village. It seems that General Markac insisted and in a way maybe even actually put the pressure on him. He wanted exact details, where, what was his direction of movement for his group. At the end, he told him, yes, that his group went through that village where the houses were on fire. And with that, Drljo also directed a few ugly word towards General Markac." Around further down that page, you say: "But it was from the start point, and once we were at the end point, it was obvious that the houses were set on fire, and it was very obvious that it was our unit who went through there. And General Markac asked him what happened and how come these houses were set on fire. And after that verbal argument or conflict, the conversation was concluded, and we went to Zagreb." Now, there's no reference whatsoever -- and you also reiterated all these in more detail in your 2005 interview. There's no reference whatsoever about any combat activity, is there?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Well, when I explained to the General what our tasks were and who went which way, then he continued talking to him. In this conversation, the group leader did not specify what axis he had taken. As a matter of fact, he showed something different since the General insisted --

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... please. I'm interrupting you because I'm running out of time. Now, my question is: You described the conversation that took place between Mr. Markac and Mr. Drljo; and right along, what you refer is the unit going through a village and the houses being set on fire. Now, let me ask you the first question: Was there any reference by Mr. Drljo, or did you hear Mr. Drljo telling Mr. Markac that they had met resistance in that village?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: I can't say 100 percent. I think that he might have done because the General himself insisted on knowing the exact details and information. And when the leader of the group in talking to him saw that the General insisted, he said that he passed by that way and that there was fighting. And he was angry in his responses, and I think he mentioned everything. And I know that on that same day, we had to establish the facts because it was obvious, it was evident that there had been contact. after that conversation, Chief Janic asked to talk to me and to them and to the members, and I don't think that anybody challenged that there had been contact and that something had, in fact, had happened and that two enemy soldiers had listen cited and that they opened fire. I think that that was established that that's what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: What did you see? What did you see at this place that made it obvious to you that there was contact? Did you see evidence of spent bullets or any indications that there has been combat, or is it the burnt houses?

utterances.speaker: JOSIP CELIC.
utterances.text: Exclusively on the basis of what the members of the groups said and who passed by that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Mahindaratne, I'm looking at the clock. We're past a quarter to 2.00. How much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MS. MAHINDARATNE
utterances.text: I believe about half an hour, Mr. President, so, perhaps, I'll resume tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There's no way that we could take that half an hour now. We'll consider the time which will be available to you. Also, I do know what the plans are for the next witness. I'm looking at you Mr. Waespi. Is the next witness available tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, she is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Prepare, Ms. Mahindaratne, for focussed, to the point, further examination, and the Chamber will consider what time will be given to you. Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, just for your planning purposes, we'll have about half an hour to an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that information. We'll further consider the matter. We'll also, of course, ask our registrar to make the correct calculations which will conclude the time that the Chamber has taken. On the basis of that information, we'll give you further guidance. I don't know whether that would still be this afternoon, but we'll try to give you it already today. Then, first of all, Mr. Celic, I instruct you that you should not speak with anyone, whoever it is, about the testimony you've given today and about the testimony that you are still expected to give tomorrow. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00 because we resume on Friday, the 5th of September, 9.00, in Courtroom I.

utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 5th day of September, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
